after: ## Language and thought: two opposite claims
alt: The strong version of Sapir-Whorf says language determines thought; the weak version says it influences thought. Carmichael's study: the same ambiguous drawing labelled eyeglasses or dumbbells was later drawn to look like its label. Berinmo and English speakers each found colours across their own language's boundaries easier to distinguish and remember, supporting the weak version.
caption: Labels and colour words influence memory and recognition: evidence for the weak version.

alt: Four cards give the functions of animal communication with examples: survival (vervet monkey alarm calls), reproduction (courtship), territory (birdsong) and food (the honeybee dance). Human language adds displacement, creativity or productivity and abstract ideas. A note says the bee dance shows only a limited form of displacement.
caption: Animals communicate for survival, reproduction, territory and food; humans can talk about anything.

alt: Left: the round dance, a looping path used when food is close, tells bees to search nearby. Right: the waggle dance for food further away; the angle of the waggle run from vertical on the comb shows the direction of food relative to the sun, and its length shows the distance.
caption: Angle shows direction; length shows distance. The round dance means food is nearby.

alt: Concentric zones around a person run from intimate distance, for close friends and family, out to public distance, for strangers and speakers. Personal space varies with culture, status and gender. An application: Kai's classmates step back because his home culture's conversational distance is smaller.
caption: Personal space runs from intimate to public, and its size depends on culture, status and gender.

alt: Two columns of evidence. Innate (Darwin): expressions helped survival, babies and children born blind show them, and an isolated culture recognised the same basic expressions. Learned: Yuki's cultural difference, personal space and gestures. Two faces show Yuki's finding: Japanese participants weighted the eyes, American participants the mouth.
caption: Some expressions are innate, but culture shapes how they are shown and read.
